title: Vatican II (1962–65)
hookLine: the Catholic Church opens its windows: Mass in local languages, new respect for other churches

cards: A small book with a ribbon in it, worn soft at the corners. It's an old Catholic missal, and on each page the prayers of the Mass run in two columns: Latin on one side, the local language on the other.
For a long time, Catholics of the Western church heard the Mass in Latin, whether they lived in Manila or Milwaukee, and followed along in books like this one.
Then a pope, John the Twenty-Third, called the bishops of the world to Rome for a council. A story often told has him opening a window to show what he hoped it would do: let in fresh air.

teach.b: The Second Vatican Council met in Rome over several autumns, and its documents changed ordinary church life. Take four of them. First, worship.

The council allowed the Mass to be said in local languages, and asked that the people take a full, active part in it, not only watch. Soon parishes around the world heard the prayers in their own tongue.
Some Catholics heard in this an echo of Pentecost in Acts, where, in the King James Bible, "every man heard them speak in his own language." Second, scripture.
The council urged that the Bible be opened wide to ordinary Catholics, read, prayed and studied, not left to the clergy. Third, other Christians.

teach.h: OTHER CHRISTIANS AS BROTHERS AND SISTERS.
teach.b: The council spoke of Protestant and Orthodox Christians with new warmth, as brothers and sisters in Christ, still separated, and called Catholics to pray and work for unity. Fourth, other faiths.
In a short document, the council said the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions.

teach.h: RESPECT FOR OTHER FAITHS, AND FOR JEWS.
teach.b: And it said plainly that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews of his time, or against Jews today, and it deplored hatred of Jews. Catholics still discuss how to read the council.

Some see a long-overdue renewal. Some feel beauty and reverence were lost along the way, and some parishes still celebrate the older Latin Mass with permission. Both groups are reading the same documents.
That's part of what a council leaves behind.

how: Catholic parishes today celebrate Mass in local languages, with readings from both Testaments, while some parishes also celebrate the older Latin form.

games.q: you're a bishop at the council. the question on the table: what language should the Mass be said in?
o: allow the local language, so the people can take part.
games.why: the council allowed local languages and asked for the people's full, active part. parishes around the world soon heard the Mass in their own tongue.

practice: Choose one of the four: the language of worship, the Bible in ordinary hands, other Christians, other faiths.

If you're Catholic, think of the words you'll hear at your next Mass in your own language; if you're not, imagine hearing the prayers at the center of someone's week in a language they understood, or didn't.
If you pray, pray in whatever words are truly yours.

wordCard.voice: Vatican II. The Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council, which brought the Mass into local languages and spoke with new respect of other churches and faiths.
